editorial_contributions.text:
The problem considered is the following: if all the points of the plane are to be colored in such a way that no two points at unit distance apart receive the same color, what is the minimum number of colors that can be used? According to Alexander Soifer who has researched the origin of the problem ``Edward Nelson created the problem and told the problem to John Isbell in 1950''. Alexander Soifer intends to produce a complete version of his findings on the origin of the problem in his upcoming book [Mathematical coloring book]. We refer to this problem as the unit- distance graph problem. The minimum number of colors needed (i.e., the answer to the unit-distance graph problem) is known to be between 4 and 7 [\textit{H. Hadwiger}, \textit{H. Debrunner} and \textit{V. Klee}, Combinatorial geometry in the plane (1964)]. The lower bound of 4 is due to \textit{L. Moser} and \textit{W. Moser} [Can. Math. Bull. 4, 187-189 (1961)].


Let \((\mathbb{R}^ n,1)\) denote the graph with vertex set \(\mathbb{R}^ n\) and two vertices adjacent if and only if their Euclidean distance is 1. A unit-distance graph in \(\mathbb{R}^ n\) is a graph that is isomorphic to a subgraph of \((\mathbb{R}^ n,1)\). The unit-distance graph problem in the plane is to determine the chromatic number \(\chi((\mathbb{R}^ 2,1))\).


In Section 2, we survey the results which are of some interest to the unit-distance graph problem. In Section 3, we consider the problem of coloring the rational subspaces up to dimension 4. In Section 4, we generalize the construction in the above-mentioned book of Hadwiger, Debrunner and Klee showing \(\chi((\mathbb{R}^ 2,1))\leq 7\). In Section 5, we consider distance graphs on integer lattices and prove several easy results. In Section 6, we construct several infinite bipartite subgraphs of the unit-distance graph.

title.title: Unit-Distance Graphs in Minkowski metric spaces

editorial_contributions.text: A graph is unit-distance if it can be drawn in the plane with all edges being segments of length 1. In this paper a new family of such graphs is constructed each requiring at least 4 colors for any vertex-coloring and having no triangular subgraphs. The smallest member of this family has only 47 vertices.

title.title: A \(4\)-chromatic unit-distance graph with no triangles

editorial_contributions.text: A unit-distance graph in \(\mathbb{R}^ n\) is a graph with a subset of \(\mathbb{R}^ n\) as the vertex set and two vertices adjacent only if their Euclidean distance is 1. It is shown that a finite graph \(G\) on \(m\) vertices is isomorhpic to a unit-distance graph in \(\mathbb{R}^ n\) if and only if there exists a real number \(\lambda\) and for arbitrarily large integers \(r\) the graph \(G\) can be drawn in the \(n\)-dimensional integer lattice \(\mathbb{Z}^ n\) such that (i) the distance between every pair of vertices is at least \(\lambda r\), and (ii) adjacent vertices have their distance in the closed interval \([r- g(r), r+ g(r)]\) with \(g(r)= 2\sqrt n/r^{1/nm}\). In the case of the Euclidean plane two variations of this result are proved.

editorial_contributions.text: A graph is (approximately) unit-distance in the metric space \(M\) if it can be drawn in \(M\) with all edges corresponding to pairs of points at distance (approximately) 1. This paper gives an overview of known results and open problems about the structure, chromatic and clique numbers of such graphs for several euclidean and real Minkowski spaces.

editorial_contributions.text: Let \(Q^ 5\) denote the collection of all the rational points in \(E^ 5\) and let \(G(Q^ 5)\) denote the graph obtained by taking \(Q^ 5\) as its vertex set and connecting 2 points iff they are at a distance 1. There is shown that the graph \(G(Q^ 5)\) has chromatic number at least 6 and clique number 4.

title.title: Maximal and minimal forbidden unit-distance graphs in the plane

editorial_contributions.text: Graphs realizable by points of euclidean plane as vertices and point pairs at unit distance as edges found interest in several problems of combinatorial geometry, among them the problem of the chromatic number of the plane. A strange characterization of unit-distance graphs was obtained by Chilakamarri who proved that a graph \(G\) is realizable as unit-distance graph in euclidean plane if and only if there is an \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that for each sufficiently large \(r\) the graph \(G\) can be realized with points of the integer lattice \(\mathbb{Z}^2\) as vertices, any two of which have distance at least \(\varepsilon r\), and two vertices \(p,q \in \mathbb{Z}^2\) are joined by an edge iff their euclidean distance is in the interval \([r - \sqrt 2,r + \sqrt 2]\). This paper continues the investigation of this class of graphs (realizable with integer lattice points, which are joined by an edge iff their distance is in the interval \([r - \sqrt 2,r + \sqrt 2])\) by determining the clique number and bounds for the chromatic number and proving a Ramsey-type result for colorings of the integer lattice.
